newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Water levels up in depleted Sri Lankan reservoirs.
newsitem.headline: Water levels up in depleted Sri Lankan reservoirs.

text.p: Water levels in Sri Lanka's depleted hydropower reservoirs rose substantially over the weekend for the first time since January after heavy rains, an official of the state power utility said on Tuesday.
"Sunday was a good day. The rains raised our storage by about 15 gigawatt hours (GwH)," said a Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) official.
Current storage was now 257 GwH, about 20 percent of the total storage capacity of 1,260 GwH, he said.

"At the moment we have no plans to impose power cuts given the additions we have made to the grid," he added. "But had we planned power cuts, this rise in water levels would have delayed them by two weeks. We can save one gigawatt hour from a one hour power cut."

Tropical Sri Lanka is facing the prospect of power cuts after water levels in hydropower resevoirs fell to dangerously low levels with the failure of the winter northeast monsoon for the second successive year and weak intermonsoon showers.
The Indian Ocean island has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectric plants, usually starts around the third week of May.
The government last week banned the use of grid electricity to run air-conditioners saying it was necessary to conserve electricity to avoid the lengthy power cuts of last year.
The island now has a permanent installed capacity of 1,135 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power, produced mainly by diesel plants.
The CEB has also added 74 megawatts to its grid from diesel power plants hired from the private sector.
New CEB power plants generating 40 MW are to be commissioned by June.
The CEB has said it plans to reduce dependence on hydropower to about 57 percent, from almost 84 percent, by mid-1997 by building more diesel plants.
